title: Diagnostic entry: matter, moles and balanced equations
summary: The chemist's bookkeeping, tested before anything new is taught: the mole and molar mass, atomic symbols and isotopes, formulas, balancing for mass and charge, reaction stoichiometry with a mass-balance check, limiting reactant and yield, molarity and dilution. Accepted attempts here are the readiness evidence for the course; advanced mathematics is not.

objectives.description: Convert between mass, amount and number of particles using molar mass and Avogadro's number, carrying units and significant figures.
Balance a chemical equation for atoms and charge, with phase labels, and read its coefficients as mole ratios.
Identify a limiting reactant by comparing amounts, compute theoretical and percent yield and the excess remaining.
Read an atomic symbol (protons, neutrons, electrons), compute an average atomic mass from isotopic abundances, and compute molarity through a dilution.
State the assumptions behind every numerical answer (purity, completeness, phases, additive volumes).

preparation.description: Read the source's own framing: lecture 1 assigns a 'Review of Fundamentals' as home reading rather than lecture material (notes page 1).
OpenStax 3.1 Formula Mass and the Mole Concept: the mole, Avogadro's number, molar mass; read Examples 3.3–3.6 as worked patterns.
OpenStax 2.3 Atomic Structure and Symbolism: symbols, isotopes, average atomic mass (Examples 2.3–2.4).
OpenStax 4.1 Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations: atom conservation, phase labels, ionic equations (Example 4.1).
OpenStax 4.3 Reaction Stoichiometry and 4.4 Reaction Yields: stoichiometric factors, limiting reactant, percent yield (Examples 4.10–4.13).

activities.title: The diagnostic lesson and the review sections
activities.instructions: Read the lesson first. For each definition, write it in your own words in the notebook with one example of your own. Then open only the OpenStax sections for the topics you did not already know; the others can wait until an exercise sends you back to them. OpenStax is read in the browser (reference-only licence); nothing from it is pasted into Corniversity.

activities.title: Diagnostic: three exercises
activities.instructions: Attempt all three exercises before asking for hints; this is a diagnostic, so an honest unaided attempt is the useful one. Write units on every quantity, state the phase of every substance and finish each exercise with the assumptions you made. Submit each attempt when complete; revise after feedback.

activities.title: Optional self-check: MIT's review problems
activities.instructions: If you want more practice after the diagnostic, MIT's own '5.111 Review Problems' PDF (significant figures, moles, mass percentage, solution preparation) is linked here with its solutions on the lecture 1 page. These are MIT's problems under CC BY-NC-SA; they are linked, not copied, and are not assessed by Corniversity.

activities.title: Say what you assumed
activities.instructions: Without the lesson open, list in the notebook the assumptions behind a mass-to-mass stoichiometry calculation and behind a dilution calculation, then say what would change in each if one assumption failed. The tutor will compare your list with the lesson's.

exitCheck.description: All three diagnostic exercises accepted: a balanced equation with a mass-balance check, a correct limiting-reactant and yield analysis, and correct isotope and molarity results, each with assumptions stated. Exercise 1 is the anchor; the course's entry rule is satisfied when all three are accepted.

commonMisconceptions.claim: An equation can be balanced by changing a subscript.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Subscripts define the substance; changing one changes which compound is meant. Only coefficients are adjusted, and both atoms and charge must balance.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The reactant present in the smaller mass is the limiting reactant.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Limiting is decided by amounts compared with the stoichiometric ratio, never by masses. A small mass of a light reactant can be in large excess.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solvent added.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of final solution. Dilution conserves the amount of solute (c1V1 = c2V2) and assumes the final volume is as stated.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The mass number is the number of neutrons, and an anion has fewer electrons than the neutral atom.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Mass number A = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z; an anion has gained electrons (Z − q with q negative gives more than Z).
